content: 1. Training clinicians in communication skills is essential to address patient concerns about prognosis, benefits, and risks of antibiotic treatments. It also helps manage self-limiting conditions and align patient expectations with clinical decisions regarding antibiotics during visits. 2. Requiring explicit written justification in medical records for prescribing antibiotics that are not recommended has been shown to reduce inappropriate prescribing by holding clinicians accountable for their decisions. 3. Clinical decision support systems, which provide specific information in electronic or print form during routine workflows, can improve diagnostic accuracy and management of common conditions. For example, they can discourage unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions for acute bronchitis in healthy adults. 4. Utilizing call centers, nurse hotlines, or pharmacist consultations as triage systems can prevent unnecessary clinic visits for conditions like the common cold that do not require in-person evaluation. 5. Tracking and reporting clinician antibiotic prescribing practices, also known as audit and feedback, can guide practice changes and assess progress in improving antibiotic use. Decisions must be made about the level of tracking (individual clinician or facility), outcomes to monitor, and data collection methods, such as electronic medical record extraction or manual chart reviews. 6. Individualized feedback to clinicians on their antibiotic prescribing practices, including comparisons with peers, is an effective way to promote adherence to evidence-based guidelines. For instance, feedback comparing a clinician’s performance to top-performing peers has been shown to reduce inappropriate prescribing. 7. Tracking high-priority conditions, such as acute bronchitis, can help assess whether antibiotics were appropriately prescribed based on diagnostic criteria, recommended agents, and correct dosing and duration. This approach has been effective in reducing inappropriate antibiotic use and improving selection. 8. Systems can also track the percentage of visits where antibiotics are prescribed by individual clinicians, providing comparisons with peers to minimize the influence of diagnostic coding differences. This helps address practices like diagnosis shifting, where a clinician may alter diagnostic codes to justify antibiotic use. 9. When comparing metrics for antibiotic stewardship, it is important to consider differences in patient populations, as some clinicians may treat patients with higher underlying needs for antibiotics, such as those with immunosuppression. 10. Certain healthcare systems may track and report complications of antibiotic use, such as Clostridioides difficile infections, drug interactions, and adverse events, as well as trends in antibiotic resistance among common outpatient bacterial pathogens. 11. In such cases, investigating C. difficile infections linked to prior outpatient visits and antibiotic prescriptions can serve as a marker for potential adverse drug events. 12. Both clinicians and clinic leaders play a role in antibiotic stewardship. Clinicians can self-evaluate their prescribing practices to align with updated evidence-based guidelines and participate in continuing medical education and quality improvement activities. 13. Outpatient clinic or healthcare system leaders can implement antibiotic prescribing tracking and reporting systems, focusing on high-priority conditions identified as opportunities for improvement. Outcomes to track may include the percentage of visits leading to antibiotic prescriptions and, for health systems, complications of antibiotic use and resistance trends. 14. Education on appropriate antibiotic use can involve both patients and clinicians, emphasizing evidence-based practices and the importance of reducing unnecessary antibiotic use to combat resistance and improve patient outcomes.
